ToolHeader.title: IP address
ToolHeader.description: Where your address points and who runs it — country, city, ISP, ASN and time zone. Look up any IPv4 or IPv6 address too. The lookup goes through our own server, so your address is never handed to a third party by your browser.

errors.invalid: That is not a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address.
errors.private: That address is private — 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x and the loopback range only exist inside a local network, so no database can place them.
errors.notFound: No provider could place this address.
errors.rateLimited: The lookup service is out of free requests for now. Try again in a few minutes.
errors.network: The lookup did not go through. Check your connection and try again.
errors.noPublicIp: Your address did not reach us — the server saw a local address instead of yours. That is normal in local development, and in production it means a proxy is not forwarding it.

map.title: Roughly here
map.noPoint: This address has no coordinates to plot.
map.accuracy: City level at best. The point is where the network operator registered the address block, which is regularly a different city and occasionally a different region — it is not a street address, and it is not where you are sitting.

privacy.title: What an IP address does and does not give away

reveals.title: What it does reveal
reveals.body: Your rough area and, reliably, who your provider is. Every site you visit sees it — it is how the reply reaches you. Combined with the values on our device info page it becomes a fingerprint that is rarely shared by two people.

hides.title: What it does not
hides.body: Your name, your address, your device and what you do online. An IP identifies a network connection, not a person. Only your provider can link it to an account, and in most countries that takes a legal request.

detection.title: Why there is no VPN check here
detection.body: Honest proxy, VPN and Tor detection needs a commercial database that every provider charges for. We do not have one, so this page does not claim to know. A tool that prints “not a proxy” without checking is worse than one that stays quiet — this page used to do exactly that, and the verdict was hardcoded.

accuracy.question: The city is wrong. Why?
accuracy.answer: Because IP geolocation is an inference, not a measurement. A database maps blocks of addresses to the place where the network operator registered them, which for a mobile network is often the operator's headquarters and for a home connection is often the nearest regional exchange. Country is usually right; city is a good guess; the coordinates are the centre of that guess, not your location.

whatItReveals.question: Can someone find me from my IP address?
whatItReveals.answer: Not on their own. They get your provider and a rough area — the same thing this page shows. Linking an address to a subscriber requires records only the provider holds, and in most countries a legal request to get them. What an IP is genuinely useful for is spotting that a login came from an unexpected country.

vpn.question: Does this show whether I am on a VPN?
vpn.answer: No, and it will not pretend to. VPN and proxy detection needs a commercial database of known exit nodes; every provider that offers it charges for it. What you can do here yourself: look up your address with the VPN off, then with it on. If the provider and the country change, the VPN is carrying your traffic.

ipv6.question: Why does my address look like 2001:4860:4860::8888?
ipv6.answer: That is IPv6. The 32-bit IPv4 space ran out, so networks moved to 128-bit addresses written as hexadecimal groups, with :: standing in for a run of zeros. Both forms work here. Geolocation for IPv6 is often less precise, because the blocks are newer and the databases have had less time to learn them.

changing.question: Why does my IP address keep changing?
changing.answer: Most home and mobile connections get a dynamic address: the provider lends you one from a pool and takes it back when your router reconnects. A fixed address is usually a paid business option. On mobile you may also share one public address with thousands of other subscribers through carrier-grade NAT, which is why two phones on the same network can look identical from the outside.

signals.title: Does your browser agree?
signals.pending: Comparing what your browser reports with what your address says…
signals.summaryAligned: Everything your browser reports matches your address. Nothing here suggests a VPN or proxy.
signals.summaryMismatched: {count} of these disagree. That is a signal, not a verdict — a VPN produces it, and so does travelling or a manually set clock.

timezone.label: Time zone
timezone.mismatch: Your operating system is set to a different zone than your address resolves to. A VPN moves your address but not your clock, which is why this is the strongest free signal there is.

offset.label: UTC offset
offset.mismatch: The actual hour difference disagrees, not just the zone name. This is the stricter version of the check above — Berlin and Paris share an offset, so a name-only difference means little.

language.label: Language region
language.mismatch: Your browser asks for content from a different country than your address is in. The weakest of the three: plenty of people browse in a language that is not their country's.
